To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

contention for memory resources is a major cause of cross-core interference in warehouse scale computers, and that contention-aware scheduling techniques can significantly reduce the interference, thereby enabling the consolidation of latency-sensitive applications.

contention for memory bandwidth can be mitigated by using compiler optimizations that reduce the memory bandwidth demand of applications, and that these optimizations can be applied to a wide range of applications.

contention for QoS can be reduced by 1) using a combination of static and dynamic techniques to improve the locality of the data that is accessed by the applications and 2) using a combination static and dynamic techniques for reducing the contention for the memory hierarchy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question: can we design a system that allows WSC operators to consolidate applications with different QoS requirements without incurring severe performance interference and without requiring any application-level changes?
enabling QoS in WSCs, where applications with different QoS needs are co-located, and contention for shared memory is managed without incurring any performance overhead.
the following question: Can we allow co-location of latency- and bandwidth-sensitive applications on multicore machines, while ensuring that their QoS is not impacted?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current practice of disallowing co-located workloads in WSCs is not sustainable in the long run.

the current state-of-the-art techniques for mitigating contention for shared resources are not sufficient to enable co-location of latency- and throughput-sensitive applications in WSCs without compromising QoS.

contention for shared resources can have severe performance interference effects on latency-sensitive workloads, but that contention for shared memory is a particularly important factor in this regard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to mitigate the performance interference caused by contention for memory resources by using a combination of compiler optimizations and operating system support.
we propose a novel technique that allows for QoS-aware co-locations of latency-sensitive workloads on multicore machines.
the contention between the applications can be reduced by making the applications more “nice”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to co-locate latency-sensitive workloads with other applications on a multicore processor without compromising their QoS.
it is possible to mitigate performance interference in WSCs without resorting to the QoS policy of isolating latency-sensitive applications.
it is possible to co-locate latency-sensitive applications with non-critical applications on a WSC machine without compromising on QoS.
